Comparing the calculated values to experimental data and ab initio simulations, it is observed that the atom-in-jellium model's accuracy significantly improves at higher pressures, ultimately yielding results comparable to those of density functional theory in pressure ranges exceeding 1 million bar, allowing for reliable predictions of shear moduli under extreme pressure conditions.

This research tackles the challenge of restoring blurred images caused by human and environmental motion using a novel algorithm. The current methods for image de-blurring are inadequate in handling blur resulting from motion, primarily because they rely on clear areas in the image for training and can only be applied to specific types of images. In contrast, our proposed algorithm employs a learning-based approach that simulates blurred images based on the blurring effects of motion, without requiring any clean areas. The algorithm consists of two key components: a blur synthesizer that generates the blurred image based on the motion and its effect on the image, and a de-blurring network that unblurs the image using the synthesized blur information. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through experiments on various datasets, with the results showing that it outperforms existing de-blurring algorithms.

The tidal disruption of stars at the supermassive black holes' event horizon produces a distinct type of transient event in the X-ray and ultraviolet parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. These occurrences are difficult to distinguish from other events such as background flares from distant galaxies or active galactic nuclei, and explosive events like supernovae or gamma-ray bursts, which is a challenge for scientists. To resolve this issue, researchers have developed a new method that uses the optical light curve of these events to distinguish between tidal disruption events and other types of transient events. This method involves using a specific statistical test to compare the light curve of these events to a known pattern of a tidal disruption event, which is known as the "observed light curve method". The researchers have tested this method on 59 known tidal disruption events and 557 impostor events, which are events that are not tidal disruption events but are similar in their light curve. The results show that the method is highly effective in distinguishing between tidal disruption events and impostors, with a high true positive rate of 98% and a low false alarm rate of 0.5%. This method can be used to identify tidal disruption events in large datasets of optical transient events, which will help scientists to understand the nature of these events and the black holes that produce them.

Using the Canada-France High-Resolution Surveys, a comprehensive analysis of the environment surrounding bright, early cosmic star-forming galaxies was conducted. By comparing the distribution of these galaxies to random points, it was discovered that 96% confidence levels indicate the presence of galaxy overdensities around 40% of the 101 selected galaxies at a 2.6% distance from them. This finding suggests that these galaxies reside within dense areas, contradicting the theory of them being isolated, scattered throughout the early universe. Furthermore, it was found that 75% of the 40 galaxies at a 1.5% to 2.5% distance from the galaxies exhibited significant overdensity, indicating a substantial number of galaxies within these dense areas. This research supports the idea that these bright galaxies are located at the center of galaxy clusters, a phenomenon observed in later stages of the universe. This study's findings are consistent with simulations of galaxy formation, which also predict the presence of dense areas surrounding these galaxies.

A comprehensive study of the reflectance spectra of 21 cold classical Trans-Neptunian objects in the near-infrared range has been conducted. These objects were discovered within the Kuiper Belt and are believed to be remnants from the period when the solar system was still in its formative stages. Analyzing the data collected from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer, researchers found that the objects exhibited a range of reflectance characteristics, with most displaying a flat or marginally inclined curve as a function of wavelength. A comparison of the objects' reflectance patterns with those of other celestial bodies revealed that the cold classical TNOs display a distinct range of reflectance characteristics, and their near-infrared properties are more similar to those of outer Solar System objects than those of main-belt asteroids. A correlation was observed between the objects' reflectance spectra and their semi-major axes, with certain objects displaying a distinct change in slope at a specific wavelength. A statistical analysis of the data, accounting for observational biases, indicates that the objects' reflectance characteristics are consistent with a bimodal distribution, with most objects falling within a relatively narrow range of reflectance values, and a smaller group with significantly higher reflectance values.

The chilly dwell test is a crucial method for assessing the load shedding and precipitation of titanium alloys at lower temperatures. This study investigates the chilly dwell behavior of a Ti-6Al alloy using the coupled finite element and crystal plasticity method. To achieve this, the initial stress-strain characteristics of the alloy are derived through digital image correlation and are then used in conjunction with the crystal plasticity model. The model is then utilized to predict the load shedding and associated load retention, which are experimentally measured using the chilly dwell test. The findings indicate that the coupled framework can effectively simulate the load shedding and retention properties of the alloy during the chilly dwell test.

Software product lines are built using feature models that define a set of user preferences. To manage complexity, feature models are often simplified through abstraction, leading to the need for model comprehension. Studies suggest that feature models with many elements are difficult to understand, and eye movements indicate that users primarily focus on specific features and connections, rather than the model's structure, particularly when processing smaller feature sets.

A new technique called StraKLIP has been developed to detect and measure faint objects located close to brighter stars, such as planets and asteroids, by analyzing images using the Karhunen-Loève transform. This method employs a unique, non-convex approach that overcomes the limitations of traditional methods, generating a map that accurately shows the relationship between observed and true object locations. In order to detect these objects, a novel mapping function based on the StraKLIP algorithm reconstructs the true object location based on the observed location, taking into account the effects of the host star's diffraction pattern and motion. The proposed framework has been tested on simulated images of Jupiter and KELT-9b, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting faint objects located very close to the host star.

The Page curve, initially describing the entropy growth of a black hole behind its horizon, has been extended to various non-equilibrium thermodynamic systems.  Researchers have also explored its application in the early universe, specifically with the cosmological horizon.  A new finding reveals that this arc is consistent with the behavior of entanglement entropy in the early universe, as seen in specific models of the early universe.  A key factor in this consistency lies in the role of the horizon as a boundary that regulates entanglement.  As a result, the page arc is a universal indicator of the presence of a boundary, which can be used to study various systems including black holes and the early universe.

We have developed a novel strategy for creating Weyl nodes in a tailored lattice structure, and our results show that these nodes can be manipulated through the application of a magnetic field. Our findings indicate that by adjusting the magnetic field strength, the Weyl nodes can either merge or split, and this transformation leads to the loss or re-emergence of Weyl nodes. Consequently, the intricate Fermi arcs associated with these nodes undergo a complete disappearance or re-appearance in accordance with the magnetic field-induced changes in the nodes. Our research utilizes a 2D photonic crystal array to experimentally verify these results.

The current state-of-the-art approach for generating long film sequences relies on pre-trained models that predict frames based on an input sequence. However, these models lack the ability to generate entire films from scratch, and their performance degrades when given fewer input frames. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method that utilizes an unsupervised technique to train a neural network on long film sequences. Inspired by the human brain's hierarchical learning process, our network consists of two main components: a high-level video understanding module and a detailed frame generation module. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our unsupervised approach in producing high-quality film sequences, even with just four input frames, and outperform existing supervised models on benchmark datasets.

Mitochondria form a complex, dynamic structure within cells, comprising numerous individual organelles interconnected by structures called tubules. Research has suggested that the physical and functional connections between these organelles play a significant role in how they evolve over time. We have developed a mathematical framework to model how genetic mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA") spread throughout the mitochondrial network, considering the impact of physical interactions between individual organelles. We have also investigated how changes in the structure of the mitochondrial network itself influence the development of genetic mutations, including the effects of breaking or forming new connections between organelles. Our research findings were validated using a computational model that simulates the behavior of individual mitochondria over time. We have also applied our model to analyze the spread of genetic mutations in human mtDNA, using data from multiple studies. We have also explored the effects of removing parts of the mitochondrial network on the development of genetic mutations, and how this may contribute to the origins of certain diseases.

We introduce Mixer-TTS, a novel non-autoregressive text-to-speech model that efficiently produces high-quality speech using lightweight supervision. Mixer-TTS is grounded in a non-autoregressive generative framework that utilizes a pre-trained language model to inform its audio generation. Unlike traditional text-to-speech models, Mixer-TTS does not rely on a pre-existing vocal synthesizer, instead leveraging a pre-trained language model to capture sentence-level linguistic features. This approach enables Mixer-TTS to produce speech that is both coherent and well-articulated. By conditioning our model on a single token, Mixer-TTS achieves rapid generation, while its use of language model embeddings and lightweight vocal data training enables a compact model size. Experimental results demonstrate that Mixer-TTS outperforms state-of-the-art non-autoregressive models, while also achieving comparable performance to more complex autoregressive models.

The crystallization process in phase-change materials Ge2Sb2Te5 has been studied using a combination of techniques, including X-ray diffraction and X-ray reflectometry.  This study aimed to determine the most suitable model for describing the material's transformation, either a standard Avrami model or a more complex one. Our results show that the most accurate description is provided by the Avrami model with a non-linear transformation, which is consistent with a nucleation and growth mechanism.  However, the analysis also revealed that the material's amorphous phase may be partially crystalline, existing in a range of crystallite sizes.

Theoretical research into the surface properties of inclined topological insulators, 
which combine both topological insulators and Weyl semimetals in a stack, 
has led to the identification of various unique surface states. These states 
include gapless Dirac cones, surface states with a gap, and Z2 interface insulator 
states. Our findings also show that the angle at which the layers are stacked 
has a significant impact on the properties of the inclined topological insulators 
and can be adjusted to control their surface properties.

The presence of a planet in a protoplanetary disk causes variations in the ice line, but its potential impact on the distribution of water-rich planets is still unclear. Using simulations of multiple disks with varying gap sizes and orbital locations, we found that gap formation significantly affects the ice line position. As a result, in some cases the ice line is pushed outward, reducing the likelihood of water-rich planet formation, and in others, it forms closer to the star, increasing their formation potential. These findings suggest that most super-Earth-forming regions may produce few water-rich super-Earth planets, and that the presence of giant planets in certain areas could lead to an overabundance of warm Neptune-like planets.

A new method for reinforcement learning has been introduced, which improves
efficiency by leveraging unlabeled examples to pinpoint the most valuable data
points. This approach, contrastive-curiosity-driven learning, uses a contrastive
learning technique to identify the most interesting examples. By implementing
this method, we enhance the learning process, and empirical tests have shown that
our method surpasses other models in efficiency, achieving better results in
multiple complex environments.

This research introduces DiaNet, a cutting-edge NLP system designed for handling intricate dialects in Arabic as spoken in everyday life. The proposed DiaNet architecture incorporates a hierarchical attention mechanism paired with multi-task learning to enhance the performance of its Transformer and pre-trained BERT components. We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the dialect, examining its distinct linguistic features and their implications on machine learning algorithms. The proposed system was evaluated using three datasets containing labeled dialectal text, speech, and the 2009 Arabic multimodal sentiment analysis challenge, with DiaNet achieving exceptional accuracy on these benchmarks.

The Strip Packing problem is a fundamental problem in Combinatorial Optimization, which involves packing a set of given objects (such as rectangles, polygons, or blocks) without overlapping them in a long, thin shape. This problem is highly versatile and can be applied to various fields, including logistics, manufacturing, and cloud storage. In this research, we focus on a specific version of the Strip Packing problem, known as Guillotine Strip Packing, which involves packing objects with a rectangular shape in a vertical, non-rotating manner. This problem is significant in both the manufacturing and cloud storage sectors. In this study, we present a new algorithm that can efficiently pack objects in a vertical, non-rotating manner and produce a packing that is at least 1.54 times efficient, which is an improvement over the previously established lower limit of 1.51.

A new, cutting-edge approach is presented to measure the mass of galaxy clusters using the Compton-y values provided by the Planck satellite. This innovative method uses a deep learning model that processes the Compton-y maps in a data-driven manner, without relying on physical models, to predict the hydrostatic mass of clusters and the associated scatter. By analyzing 143 GHz Compton-y maps, the proposed method was trained and tested on X-ray-calibrated clusters with values of Y_2005 between 3 and 200. The results show a strong correlation between the hydrostatic mass calculated using this deep learning method and the true mass, with a high correlation coefficient (r=0.96) and a lower scatter (0.08 log M) when compared to the standard halo model-based mass estimation. The proposed method also successfully removed bias in the mass estimation, particularly for clusters with high Compton-y values. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of deep learning models in improving the accuracy of mass estimation for galaxy clusters and sets the stage for further research using these models.

Traditionally, collocations are defined as the way words fit together in language. Collocations are typically identified by the combination of two words, such as "walk in the rain." However, this approach overlooks other types of collocations, like phrases and longer phrases like "hard to walk in the rain." This paper proposes a new approach to recognizing and using collocations that goes beyond just pairs of words. The method involves breaking down text into smaller, more meaningful units called collocation tokens. These tokens consist of groups of words that are treated as a single entity when applying latent Dirichlet allocation models. The method was tested on real-world data and showed that this new approach can improve the accuracy of a range of latent Dirichlet allocation models.

The pulsar community has long been puzzled by the reservation phenomenon, where gamma-ray pulsars' arduity in transitioning to rotation-powered pulsars is unexpectedly high. Researchers have proposed various theories, such as a two-zone radiation mechanism, which has proven to be effective in accounting for the observed data. However, due to the complexity and time constraints, researchers often simplify models and rely on likelihood-based inference, which may result in biased estimation of model parameters. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to tackle the reservation puzzle by harnessing the power of Bayesian inference. We develop a probabilistic model that incorporates a Bayesian framework, which enables us to quantify the uncertainty in the model parameters and compare the performance of different models using standard Bayesian metrics. We apply our method to a dataset of 88 pulsars, and the results demonstrate that the two-zone model outperforms the single-zone model, which supports the theoretical model's efficacy.

We introduce the Fourier and Fourier--Stieltjes *-algebras for Fell structures over discrete groups and explore their foundational properties. Notably, when the groups in question are restricted to finite groups, we establish that the associated Fourier--Stieltjes *-algebra is isometric to the algebra of functions with compact support.

This research paper focuses on developing a novel shift-invariant space, denoted as $H_{\sigma}^r(\mathbb{C}^2)$, and its associated reproducing kernel. We introduce the circular Prolate Spheroidal Sequence (CPSSe) as a natural orthonormal basis for the shifted, truncated Hankel outer space, $H_{\sigma}^r(\mathbb{C}^2)$, derived from the shift-invariant space. We also demonstrate that a detailed analysis of the maximal support of the CPSSe is essential for efficient approximation in the shifted, truncated space $H_{\sigma}^r_N(\mathbb{C}^2)$. Furthermore, we derive the key characteristics of the CPSSe, including the optimal time-frequency localization property, and provide a detailed description of the efficient approximation in the shifted, truncated space $H_{\sigma}^r_N(\mathbb{C}^2)$.

The analysis of atomic structures using diffraction data is hindered by background noise in the data, and this noise can also be present in datasets used for training generative models that can produce atomic structures. This noise can be particularly problematic when it is similar to the signal being measured. We have developed a noise removal approach that uses a denoising score network to reduce background noise in diffraction intensities. This method is effective even when the noise and signal are closely related, and it can also be used to remove noise in training datasets to improve the robustness of generative models to noise in the data. We have evaluated the effectiveness of our score-based denoising approach using both experimental datasets and simulated data, and found that it produces accurate atomic structures from noisy datasets.

The Lagrangian transport model can effectively track changes in ocean circulation and mixing patterns by simulating the movement of virtual particles over time. By studying these virtual particles, researchers can better understand ocean dynamics, which is particularly crucial for predicting water quality and pollutant dispersion. This article presents a transport model based on Eulerian-Lagrangian hybrid data assimilation. It combines the benefits of both transport models and observation data to estimate the movement of these virtual particles. By integrating this model with the ocean data from the ARGO global network, researchers can generate reliable statistics on particle movement and mixing at both local and global levels. By applying this model to the ocean, researchers found that the Eulerian model significantly outperformed the Lagrangian model in replicating particle movement. Moreover, the model revealed that the mixing times of particles in the ocean are unexpectedly long, which is driven by the ocean's mesoscale circulation patterns.

To understand the viscosity-temperature correlation in polymeric glass-forming liquids, we use the Mie equation of state and a derived entropic theory of liquid dynamics (ETLD). The ETLD model explains liquid relaxation on the equilibrium side, linking temperature-dependent viscosity behavior to entropy density and molecular structure. The temperature-dependent viscosity pattern is predicted by calculating the equilibrium entropy density as a function of temperature. The derived results are verified by comparing simulated and measured viscosity data of the Mie Lennard-Jones mixture.

This research focuses on integrable difference equations of a scalar integrable continuous model, particularly the altered Camassa-Holm equation with a linear dispersion term (ACH). We develop a semi-discrete version of the ACH equation, demonstrating its equivalence to a discrete integrable system. Key characteristics of this discrete system include its bi-Hamiltonian structure, conservation laws, and Lax representation. Additionally, the inverse problem and discrete soliton solutions are explored.

In this research, we examine a quantum theory known as "extended" versions of de Broglie-Bohm-Bell, focusing on how it handles spin and "anyonic" systems. This theory is distinct because it doesn't rely on a hidden variable representing a spinless particle carrying a spin, but instead, it considers spin as a manifestation of a particle's self-interaction. This perspective allows our model to satisfy Bell's inequality without compromising either the EPR criterion or the principle of definite position. Furthermore, our model demonstrates that any violations of Bell's inequality in spin measurements are contingent upon the specific settings used in the experiment, thus resolving a long-standing issue with quantum contextuality.

Theoretical models of gravastars and ultracompact objects suggest the possibility of stable, compact objects with mass greater than the Schwarzschild limit but smaller than the Casper horizon, which could form in the aftermath of a supernova explosion. Researchers have proposed that compact stars, including gravastars, could be part of binary systems and contribute to the evolution of compact binaries. In this study, we investigate the secular dynamics of compact binaries consisting of a compact star, such as a black hole, gravastar, boson giant, or neutron star, orbiting around another component, which can be the same as the compact star or of a different nature. We derive the equations of motion for the binary system and its constituent parts, including the orbital frequency, spin, quadrupole, and individual component spins, and calculate the evolution of the binary's orbital frequency, spin, and quadrupole moments. We also determine the maximum and minimum values of the binary's orbital frequency and spin, and find that the dynamics of the binary system depend on the compact star's mass, which can reach up to 20 times the Schwarzschild limit. Our results provide a general understanding of the dynamics of compact binaries and can be used to study the behavior of these systems, including the emission of gravitational waves and the potential for energy extraction.

This paper introduces the "YOLO" model, a fast object recognition system that eliminates the need for individual bounding boxes at training and inference stages. By concurrently detecting multiple overlapping boxes of all sizes that encompass an entire scene, "YOLO" achieves superior accuracy and efficiency compared to existing object detection methods. "YOLO" is evaluated on the VOC2012 dataset and outperforms all other detection methods in terms of accuracy, while significantly accelerating processing speed due to its novel approach.

The Minho Citation Index is a comprehensive, citational bibliographic resource covering academic publications from the early 19th century to the present. It offers a unique search interface, as well as advanced tools for citation analysis and studying the historical development of scientific knowledge. Following a thorough quality control process, the Minho Citation Index encompasses a vast database of approximately 110 million citations and 155 million cited works.

In data analysis, decision trees and random forests are widely used methods, primarily to predict outcomes or identify key variables, often chosen for their ease of interpretation and efficiency. However, these techniques have limitations, making them less than fully comprehensive tools. Building upon the decision concept framework, researchers have developed an innovative approach that enhances these methodologies. This framework enables the construction of decision trees and random forests, offering improvements over traditional forms with new characteristics such as (1) enhanced interpretability, (2) increased precision, and (3) superior applicability to complex datasets.

The field of machine learning has seen remarkable progress, with the adoption of sophisticated neural networks in various applications, from computer vision to language comprehension. However, this surge in complex models is at odds with a corresponding emphasis on evaluating their reliability and safety; conventional evaluation methods primarily focus on their performance, not their ability to generalize correctly in real-world scenarios. In an effort to bridge this assessment gap, we introduce a framework that enables researchers to assess and evaluate neural networks based on their performance in simulated and controlled settings, while also exploring potential avenues to address these assessment gaps.

In real-world settings, various tasks are complicated by a significant imbalance in data, with a small, underrepresented target class among a plethora of more abundant non-target data points. A significant challenge arises when training data continues to grow, with new instances of the target class added incrementally, requiring models to adapt in real-time. This scenario is addressed in a new task known as continual adaptive rare-class classification, where the target class gradually evolves over time and competing models must be trained and updated in an online, memory-efficient manner using only the latest data points. A novel benchmark task has been developed to facilitate research into this scenario, with a new method called Hierarchical Adaptive Rare-class Classification Network (HARCN) proposed to tackle this task. HARCN employs a hierarchical approach, utilizing a deep neural network that incorporates a memory unit with two levels of abstraction, to effectively recognize the evolving target class. A theoretical analysis is provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of HARCN's hierarchical framework, along with experimental results showing the superiority of HARCN over state-of-the-art approaches in various real-world and synthetic datasets.

In ptychography, a focused probe induces high signal and detailed information about the sample's structure through the application of the phase problem. However, the probe's focus leads to a notable issue known as focused probe ptychography (FPP), which is the reversal of contrast between the sample and the probe. This problem is addressed in this study by developing a straightforward, yet universal, inversion method to resolve the issue. The proposed approach is applied to a gold nanotriangle sample and demonstrates a reliable inversion of the ptychographic wavefields. The outcome of the study showcases the effectiveness of the new inversion method and highlights its potential for applications in materials science, particularly in analyzing local atomic structure.

In stochastic thermodynamics, researchers have been studying the behavior of stochastic forces and currents in the presence of fluctuations.  Although the currents in the system are typically defined by the rates of work or heat absorption across specific boundaries, these local measurements are subject to fluctuations.  To address this issue, we are developing a comprehensive framework to understand the behavior of currents in the system, particularly when the local measurements are subject to fluctuations.  In this first part of our two-part series, we are examining the properties of limiting statistics for steady-state systems, particularly when the stochastic currents are expressed in gauge-invariant forms.  Our analysis reveals that the limiting statistics of the currents are unaffected by the choice of gauge, regardless of the distribution of the local measurements.  We also demonstrate that the joint moments of the currents and the work flux can be expressed in gauge-invariant forms, and that the limiting currents are unaffected by fluctuations in the boundaries.  Our findings have significant implications for understanding the behavior of stochastic currents in the presence of fluctuations.

Recurrent neural networks, a type of model inspired by how brains learn, have been found to excel at tasks that require temporal patterns, such as predicting the next note in a piece of music or predicting the next digit in a sequence. A key aspect of these models is the use of a central node, often referred to as a "reservoir", which retains information between updates. The effectiveness of these models depends heavily on the characteristics of this reservoir, and research has shown that incorporating information from a complex system with varied temporal responses can significantly improve temporal pattern prediction capabilities. However, the underlying reasons for this improvement are not yet well understood. In this study, we investigate the relationship between the complexity of a reservoir and the accuracy of a recurrent neural network in predicting time-series data. We found that the predictive accuracy of these models is directly correlated with the level of complexity in the reservoir, including its topological features and connectivity. The findings of this study provide new insights into the relationship between the structure and performance of neural networks, and highlight the importance of considering the characteristics of the reservoir when designing these models for specific tasks.

We explore the impact of Efimov trimers on the transition dynamics of a three-particle Bose-Fermi mixture trapped in a one-dimensional potential well, which is suddenly reduced in depth.  Using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, we demonstrate that Efimov states can facilitate a Bose-Fermi transition, even when the initial state is a single fermion in a two-particle Efimov state.  Notably, Efimov states can also facilitate a Bose-Bose transition when the initial state is a two-particle Efimov state.  Furthermore, we find that Efimov states can also facilitate a Bose-Fermi transition when the initial state is a two-particle Efimov state.  The results show that Efimov states can facilitate a transition from a two-particle Efimov state to a Bose-Fermi state.

A novel approach to evaluating the quality of quantum kernels is presented, 
involving a technique inspired by the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference pattern. 
This proposed HOM test is compatible with current technological capabilities 
and demonstrates high efficiency, with a time complexity that is linear with 
the number of training samples and logarithmic with its square. Moreover, the 
HOM test is proven to be accurate even when working with imperfect data, 
including noisy training samples.

Several numerical methods have been developed to rapidly evaluate the Newtonian potential on a flat surface, with some methods offering speed and others delivering high accuracy. This work introduces a new approach that combines these benefits and adapts to complex boundary shapes within flat surfaces, also allowing for efficient computation of potential derivatives.
